sections.h2: How does selling a house work across Minnesota's 87 counties?
sections.html:
Minnesota is divided into 87 counties, and almost every step of a home sale touches a county office. Staffing, appointment rules and turnaround times differ from one courthouse to the next, so the same sale can feel different in Edina than in Aitkin.

Three county offices matter most to a seller. The assessor sets the value and classification used for your tax bill. The auditor-treasurer collects the tax and receives the certificate of real estate value when a deed changes hands. The recorder files the deed.

We keep a page for each county we cover, listed further down. For the largest metro counties, start with the Hennepin County recorder guide, the Ramsey County recorder guide or the Dakota County recorder guide.

sections.h2: How do property taxes work when you sell a house in Minnesota?
sections.html:
Property tax is paid in two halves. For most parcels over $100 in tax, the first half is due before May 16 and the second before October 16, according to Minn. Stat. 279.01. Late payment adds a penalty. On a homestead the penalty starts at 2 percent and can climb to 8 percent by the end of the year, while a nonhomestead parcel starts at 4 percent and can reach 12 percent.

That gap matters if you own a rental or a vacant house. A property that lost its homestead status after the owner moved out can carry the higher penalty schedule. Class 1b and 2a agricultural homestead property, and rural vacant land that is part of an agricultural homestead, have a different rule for the second half, which can be paid by November 15 without penalty.

If tax is owed at closing, the title company normally pays it out of the sale proceeds. Our Minnesota property tax guide explains appeals and what to do when a bill is behind. For county-specific offices, see the Hennepin, Anoka and Olmsted guides.

See also our homestead guide.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a deed and pay transfer taxes in Minnesota?
sections.html:
Two charges show up on most sales. The first is the county recorder fee, which Minn. Stat. 357.18 sets at $46 for indexing and recording a deed or other instrument. A certified copy of a record costs $10 under the same section.

The second is the state deed tax. Under Minn. Stat. 287.21, the tax is 0.0033 of the net consideration when that amount is over $3,000. When there is no consideration, or $3,000 or less, the tax is a flat $1.65. Net consideration leaves out any lien or encumbrance that remains after the sale.

A certificate of real estate value goes to the county auditor in the county where the house sits. Under Minn. Stat. 272.115, the grantor, the grantee or an agent for either files it when the deed is presented for recording, and it applies to sales for more than $3,000.

  • Ask the recorder how the office accepts deeds.
  • Have the legal description and parcel number ready.

Our quitclaim deed guide and transfer on death deed guide cover the two deed types owners ask about most.

sections.h2: How does foreclosure work in Minnesota, and how long do you have?
sections.html:
Minnesota's Chapter 580 sets out foreclosure by advertisement. Under Minn. Stat. 580.03, the notice is published for six weeks, and a copy must be served at least four weeks before the sale. Notices under sections 580.041 and 580.042 go out at the same time.

The sale is not the end of the road. Minn. Stat. 580.23 gives a default redemption period of six months after the sale, during which the owner can redeem by paying the sale price. The period stretches to 12 months if the property meets certain listed conditions, including conditions tied to the mortgage date, the size of the parcel, agricultural use, the balance compared with the original principal and reverse mortgages. Read the statute or ask an attorney which period applies to your loan.

Many owners who have a notice in hand want to sell before the sale date or before redemption runs out. The sooner you act, the more choices you keep.

  • Find the sale date and redemption deadline in your paperwork.
  • Ask your lender for a payoff figure in writing.
  • Talk to a housing counselor or attorney about reinstatement and redemption.

sections.h2: What happens to an inherited house in Minnesota?
sections.html:
An inherited house usually passes through probate before it can be sold, though a few paths skip it. A transfer on death deed, if one was recorded before the owner died, can move the property outside probate. Our Minnesota probate guide walks through the court steps.

The small estate affidavit is limited to personal property. Under Minn. Stat. 524.3-1201, a successor may collect it 30 days after death if the entire probate estate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $75,000 and no application for a personal representative is pending. It does not by itself cover a house.

Inherited sales also get a break on disclosure. Minn. Stat. 513.54 lists transfers to heirs or devisees of a decedent, and transfers by foreclosure or deed in lieu, among those where the seller disclosure rules do not apply. Estates above $3,000,000 face a separate filing, which our estate tax page covers.

sections.h2: What must a Minnesota seller disclose about the house?
sections.html:
For most residential sales, the seller must give the buyer a written disclosure before signing the purchase agreement. Minn. Stat. 513.55 says it must cover all material facts the seller knows that could significantly and adversely affect an ordinary buyer's use and enjoyment of the property, and it must be made in good faith.

Two topics have their own statutes:

  • Radon. Under Minn. Stat. 144.496, the seller discloses any knowledge of radon levels, past tests, reports and mitigation, and hands over the Department of Health publication "Radon in Real Estate Transactions." The Department of Health says more than two in five Minnesota homes have radon levels that pose a significant health risk, and that the action level is 4 pCi/L.
  • Wells. Under Minn. Stat. 103I.235, the seller states in writing whether the property has known wells, and if there are none, the deed can carry a statement that the seller does not know of any.

Section 513.54 exempts several kinds of sale, including transfers by foreclosure, transfers to heirs, and transfers to a tenant already in possession.

sections.h2: Can you sell a Minnesota house that has tenants?
sections.html:
Yes, and the buyer takes the house subject to the tenant's rights. Minnesota's rules depend on how the tenancy began and whether a foreclosure is involved.

Minn. Stat. 504B.285 covers tenants in a foreclosed home. When the lease began after the mortgage date and before redemption expired, the successor owner must give at least 90 days' written notice to vacate, provided the tenant pays rent and follows the lease. A bona fide lease running more than 90 days beyond redemption can generally run to its end, with an exception if the new owner will live there.

Outside foreclosure, your lease terms and notice rules control. Our landlord and tenant guide, eviction notice guide and eviction process page lay out the steps.

sections.h2: What does a cash, as-is sale mean in Minnesota?
sections.html:
It means the buyer purchases the house in its current condition and does not ask you to repair, clean or update it first. You still sign a purchase agreement, the title is checked, and the deed is recorded with the county.

As-is does not erase your disclosure duty. Unless your sale falls under an exception in Minn. Stat. 513.54, you still give the written disclosure, including radon and well information.

We buy houses across Minnesota in places as different as Minneapolis, Duluth and Moorhead, and the county lists below link to each local page.

faqs.q: How many counties are in Minnesota?
faqs.a: Minnesota has 87 counties. The county where the house sits decides which offices you call.

faqs.q: When are Minnesota property taxes due?
faqs.a: For most parcels the first half is due before May 16 and the second half before October 16. Penalties apply after those dates.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a deed in Minnesota?
faqs.a: The statutory county recorder fee is $46 for indexing and recording a deed. Deed tax is 0.0033 of net consideration over $3,000, with a $1.65 minimum.

faqs.q: How long is the redemption period after a Minnesota foreclosure sale?
faqs.a: The default is six months after the sale, and it is 12 months if the property meets the conditions in Minn. Stat. 580.23.

faqs.q: Do I need to disclose radon when I sell?
faqs.a: In most residential sales, yes. The seller discloses what they know about radon levels, tests and mitigation before signing the purchase agreement. Some transfers, such as to heirs, are exempt.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house with a tenant in it?
faqs.a: Yes. The buyer takes it subject to the lease, and foreclosure cases can bring a 90 day notice rule. See the tenant section above.
